Super Micro Computer (SMCI) plunged 11.3% on Thursday to close at $26.99 after word emerged that Manhattan federal prosecutors are examining whether entities linked to Alice Huang helped smuggle the company's servers into China, extending a roughly 31% one-month slide.

Yet the most telling detail may be what didn't move — peers Dell (DELL) and HPE (HPE) held steady during the selloff, suggesting investors are isolating compliance fears in Super Micro rather than punishing the AI server category as a whole. That divergence is the real story behind Thursday's rout.

The drop also came alongside a leadership crisis at Nvidia (NVDA) and Jensen Huang's resignation, adding another layer of turbulence for an AI hardware supply chain already on edge. SMCI has opened weak again today, off 2% in the early going.

SMCI with exponential daily moving averages.
A New Probe on Top of an Old Overhang

The new investigation compounds an existing legal overhang that includes the March indictment of co-founder Wally Liaw over roughly $2.5 billion in allegedly diverted servers, as well as a guilty plea from a former contractor.

Friday brought fresh pressure as documents surfaced showing 52 Super Micro units with H100 or H200 chips among servers pledged as collateral by a Shanghai firm founded by Alice Huang and later controlled by her sister, while Singapore publicly faulted the company for limited cooperation with its investigation.

Super Micro Pushes Back

Super Micro maintains that it sold the identified servers in compliance with export laws, has never counted Megaspeed as a customer, and has not received any new notice from US agencies. Those claims put the burden on prosecutors, who have yet to signal whether charges will follow.

Management also points to an August independent review that cleared current senior leadership of involvement in the earlier diversion scheme — a defense that so far hasn't stopped the stock from bleeding.

SMCI's Growth Engine Is Still Roaring

Fiscal first-quarter revenue ballooned 298% to $19.9 billion, and management raised full-year guidance to a range of $72 billion to $82 billion. That top-line surge stands in sharp contrast to a share price that has shed nearly a third of its value in just a month.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) clawed back a fraction of Thursday's 11.3% drop after denying that Singapore cloud provider Megaspeed was a customer.

The AI server maker closed at $26.99 and rose about 1.7% in after-hours trading, according to TipRanks. The rebound followed reports of a U.S. Justice Department inquiry that puts Super Micro's export controls back in focus just days after an earnings beat.

SMCI GF Value chart

Super Micro sells high-performance servers, storage systems and liquid-cooled racks to cloud providers, data center operators and other businesses. Its AI systems combine chips from suppliers such as Nvidia with networking and cooling equipment.

Bloomberg reported that U.S. investigators are examining whether entities linked to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang were involved in efforts to divert Super Micro products to China. In a statement cited by TipRanks, Super Micro said Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer.

The company said it cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials and voluntarily provided information to Singapore. Singapore's government said the company had provided limited cooperation.

The scrutiny comes as Super Micro's sales are accelerating. Fiscal first-quarter revenue nearly quadrupled year over year to about $19.9 billion, and adjusted gross margin rose to 12.8% from 9.5% a year earlier.

Investors Takeaway

The next earnings report will show whether Super Micro can deliver on its $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion quarterly sales forecast. Gross margin and operating cash flow will show how much of that growth translates into profit and cash.

Any official update that clarifies the scope of the inquiry could matter sooner. Additional checks on resellers or end customers could delay shipments and push revenue into later quarters. Meeting guidance while holding margins would give investors an early indication of whether the scrutiny is affecting deliveries.

How Much Of Dell Stock Is A Bet On Nvidia?

The laptop on your desk at work may be a Dell, but the money is now in the data center. On Monday, Nov 9, Nvidia fell 4.3% and Dell rose 5.4%. On Wednesday, after CoreWeave beat, Dell jumped 11.8% while Nvidia added 2.9%. All this while Nvidia sits 31% below its Oct 6 peak. On Thursday, the day Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, Nvidia fell 4.3% while Dell slipped 0.7%. So how much of Dell is really a bet on Nvidia?

On paper, Dell is deeply tied to Nvidia's customers. In the quarter to Jul 31, Dell's server, storage and networking unit sold $31.8 billion of its $47.0 billion of revenue, about two-thirds, up 89% from a year earlier; PCs and other client devices sold $15.0 billion. In the first half of the fiscal year that unit's sales more than doubled, from $27.1 billion to $60.8 billion. AI servers alone sold $16.4 billion, about 35% of revenue, and Dell expects $74 billion of its $192 billion this year, about 39%. Many of those servers carry Nvidia chips, some AMD's.

That 39% is easy to miss. For families with seven figures invested, Dell, Nvidia and the AI funds that hold both often add up to one bet on the same build-out. Do you know your total? A Trefis partner firm can add it up with you in a free 30-minute call.

Does The Stock Trade Like Nvidia?

Not much. Over the past year, Dell's daily moves tracked Nvidia's loosely, less than Super Micro's did.

The market prices Dell as the AI build-out, not as Nvidia: as the CoreWeaves of the world spend, Dell ships. We set out which stocks do take the hit in 5 Biggest Losers From Nvidia's $740 Billion CEO Crisis.

What If The Link Is Tighter Than It Looks?

Test the other side. If buyers move some orders to AMD, Dell still builds the server; it sells AI servers on both Nvidia and AMD chips. AMD is up 30.3% since Nov 6, and Dell rose with it. So the risk is the build-out pausing, not who runs Nvidia. But the link is loose, not absent: on Nov 10 Dell fell 3.4% as Nvidia fell 5.5%. And if the leadership change disrupts Nvidia's supply or pricing, Dell's delivery timing and its server unit's margin move with it: that unit kept 11.7% of sales as operating profit last fiscal year, against 5.6% for PCs.
